## The same eight notes, now chasing themselves

[Lesson 55](55-capstone-solo-melody.qmd) gave that setup phrase a shape. [Lesson 56](56-capstone-b-melody-accompaniment.qmd) gave it a floor to stand on.
This one hands it to a second voice and starts them two beats apart.

`[:e4, :g4, :a4, :b4, :d5, :b4, :a4, :g4]` still. E minor pentatonic was chosen
back in the setup buffer because nothing in it can clash, and that decision pays
off exactly here: a canon needs every vertical combination to work, and a
pentatonic collection has no semitones in it to go wrong.

Two voices means your representation has to hold two views at once. Each voice
needs its own events, measure references, motive labels and uncertainty markers.
Combined playback then has to reproduce the vertical coordination. Go back to
the independent-voice model in
[Lesson 47](../10-texture-and-arrangement/47-independent-voices.qmd) and the
entry-delay analysis in
[Lesson 51](../10-texture-and-arrangement/51-canon-imitation.qmd) before you
start.

## Two lines, one entry delay

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 86

# The setup phrase, one note per beat, as the subject.
upper = [
  {note: 64, start: 0.0, duration: 1.0, motive: :subject},
  {note: 67, start: 1.0, duration: 1.0, motive: :subject},
  {note: 69, start: 2.0, duration: 1.0, motive: :subject},
  {note: 71, start: 3.0, duration: 1.0, motive: :subject},
  {note: 74, start: 4.0, duration: 2.0, motive: :peak},
  {note: 71, start: 6.0, duration: 1.0, motive: :cadence},
  {note: 67, start: 7.0, duration: 1.0, motive: :cadence}
]

# The same subject an octave down, entering two beats late.
lower = [
  {note: 52, start: 0.0, duration: 2.0, motive: :support},
  {note: 52, start: 2.0, duration: 1.0, motive: :subject},
  {note: 55, start: 3.0, duration: 1.0, motive: :subject},
  {note: 57, start: 4.0, duration: 1.0, motive: :subject},
  {note: 59, start: 5.0, duration: 1.0, motive: :subject},
  {note: 62, start: 6.0, duration: 1.0, motive: :peak},
  {note: 52, start: 7.0, duration: 1.0, motive: :cadence}
]

define :play_events do |events, synth_name, amp, pan_position|
  use_synth synth_name
  cursor = 0.0
  events.each do |event|
    sleep event[:start] - cursor
    play event[:note], release: event[:duration] * 0.82,
      amp: amp, pan: pan_position
    cursor = event[:start]
  end
  sleep events.last[:duration]
end

# Every attack in either voice is a vertical event worth inspecting.
define :verticals do |top, bottom|
  onsets = (top + bottom).map { |event| event[:start] }.uniq.sort
  onsets.map do |moment|
    sounding = lambda do |voice|
      event = voice.reverse.find { |e| e[:start] <= moment }
      event && event[:start] + event[:duration] > moment ? event[:note] : nil
    end
    high = sounding.call(top)
    low = sounding.call(bottom)
    [moment, high && low ? high - low : nil]
  end
end

ends = [upper, lower].map { |v| v.last[:start] + v.last[:duration] }
raise "voices end at different times: #{ends}" unless ends.uniq.length == 1

verticals(upper, lower).each { |moment, gap| puts "beat #{moment}: #{gap}" }

in_thread { play_events upper, :piano, 0.8, -0.3 }
play_events lower, :pluck, 0.7, 0.3
```

Read the log before you judge the sound. Every vertical gap is 9, 12, 15, 16 or
17 semitones: sixths, octaves, tenths and elevenths. No seconds, no sevenths.
That isn't skill, it's the pentatonic collection doing the work, and it's the
reason this scale is where beginners are pointed.

Now listen. Can you follow the lower voice once the upper reaches its peak? The
pan settings help. So does the second synth.

## Make the coordination harder

1. Change the lower voice's entry from beat 2 to beat 1. Every vertical
   relationship shifts, and the imitation gets tighter and harder to track. Run
   `verticals` again and compare the two lists before deciding which you prefer.
2. Give both voices the same synth and set both pans to 0. The pitches and
   timings are untouched, and the two lines become much harder to separate.
   Timbre and space were doing more work than the notes were.
3. Move the lower voice's peak D from beat 6 to beat 5, colliding with the upper
   voice's held D5. Two octaves of the same pitch class at once. The alignment
   check still passes, because it only looks at endings.

## What the two views each catch

Bar totals inside one voice catch horizontal errors: a missing tie, a dotted
value entered plain. They're blind to everything vertical. A pitch can be
perfectly correct within its own line and enter a beat early against the other
one, changing the interval and the implied harmony without breaking a single
total.

That's why `verticals` exists. It rebuilds what's actually sounding at every
onset in either voice, which is a different question from what either array says
on its own. The `sounding` lambda searches backwards for the last event that
started at or before the moment, then checks it hasn't already finished. Rests
and held notes both fall out of that correctly.

Motive labels are analytical claims about the events, not instructions to the
renderer. Playback consumes `:note`, `:start` and `:duration` and ignores
`:motive` entirely. Keep it that way. The moment your labels start affecting the
sound, you can no longer revise an interpretation without editing the music.

The alignment check earns its place by being narrow and honest about it. It
proves both voices end together and nothing else, as variation 3 demonstrates.
A check that quietly seemed to cover more would be worse than this one.

## Build your own two-voice excerpt

Pick a two-voice invention, canon or contrapuntal excerpt whose lines you can
follow separately and together. Encode each voice with its own events, measure
references, motive labels and uncertainty markers, and record the source
properly using the ledger from [Lesson 42](../09-transcription/42-finding-music-you-can-legally-use.qmd).

Validate each voice horizontally first, then run something like `verticals`
across the pair and inspect every interval at every attack. Where a vertical
looks wrong, you now have two candidates: a wrong pitch, or a right pitch in the
wrong place. Write down which one you concluded and why, because in three months
that reasoning is the only part you won't be able to reconstruct.
